ut_man_size.blurb: Man Size is a cluster of big sandstone boulders along the Right Fork road in Joe's Valley, and it is bouldering only. The rock is textured but kind to skin, and landings are generally good. Problems span a very wide range, from easy to the upper double digits, with the bulk in the low and middle grades up to about V8. Joe's Valley favors powerful, gymnastic movement, and this is one of the more popular stops in the canyon. Sandstone here loses a lot of strength when damp, so wait a couple of days after rain or snow before pulling on anything.
ut_man_size.parking_note: Drive up the Right Fork road, about 0.9 miles from the canyon mouth. The largest roadside pullout on the fork serves the boulders, with a campground area and portable toilets at the same spot.

ut_battle_of_the_bulge_buttress.blurb: Battle of the Bulge Buttress is a sandstone wall at the mouth of Donnelly Canyon in Indian Creek, and the climbing is almost entirely crack trad. Most lines fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with a handful of 5.9s and a few low 5.13s, so it suits climbers who already feel at home jamming. Because the average grade runs a bit harder than next door, it tends to be quieter than the neighboring Supercrack Buttress. Bring a full rack with plenty of cams and tape for your hands. Sun reaches the wall for much of the day in high season, and wet sandstone is fragile, so give it time to dry after storms.
ut_battle_of_the_bulge_buttress.parking_note: Use the large lot at the mouth of Donnelly Canyon, shared with Supercrack Buttress, a bit over four miles beyond Newspaper Rock. A smaller pullout a few hundred feet farther along the road sits across from the middle of the wall.
ut_battle_of_the_bulge_buttress.approach: The trail from the main lot reaches the right-hand (south) end of the wall. From the pullout down the road, a cairned path leads to about the center of the cliff.

ut_cabbage_patch.blurb: Cabbage Patch is a roadside group of granite boulders on the north side of Little Cottonwood Canyon, a short drive up from the valley. Only bouldering is found here. Problems range from easy to V12, but most sit in the V1 to V5 band, so there is plenty for a mixed group. Many of the boulders are visible from the road through the trees, which keeps approaches to almost nothing, and the area is still not fully developed. Because it sits at the foot of the canyon on a busy road, traffic noise and weekend crowds are part of the experience.
ut_cabbage_patch.parking_note: Pull off along the canyon road about a quarter mile uphill from the Secret Garden boulders, on the north side. The boulders stand just inside the trees from the roadside.
ut_cabbage_patch.approach: Roughly a twenty-foot walk from the road into the trees.

vt_main_cliff_3.blurb: Main Cliff is a single-pitch granite face at Black Mountain in Vermont's Northeast Kingdom, known for crack systems and airy arêtes. It is mostly a trad crag with a smaller number of bolted lines, and the bulk of the routes fall between 5.9 and 5.11. A leaning block forms a cave near the start of the cliff, with an easy warm-up nearby. It is a remote, quiet place with no facilities, so bring a full rack with plenty of cams and be ready for changing weather. The trail in can be soggy in spring.
vt_main_cliff_3.parking_note: From VT 114 about three miles north of Norton, turn onto Gaudette Road and follow the powerline access road for 6.4 miles to a small clearing on the east side. The road can wash out, so higher clearance is wise.
vt_main_cliff_3.approach: A flagged and cairned trail leads from the far end of the clearing through recently logged ground to the right side of the cliff.

vt_marshfield_ledge.blurb: Marshfield Ledge is a large granite cliff on state forest land in central Vermont, with both trad and sport climbing. The main face offers long, multi-pitch slabs and cracks, mostly from 5.8 to 5.11, while a separate steep sport ledge higher up holds the hardest lines in the area. Many of the slab routes have bolted anchors. Friction slabs stay wet for a while after rain, so a dry spell makes for a much better day, and the sport wall is the better rainy-weather fallback. The walk in is long enough that it feels remote.
vt_marshfield_ledge.parking_note: On VT 232, a little past the Kettle Pond parking heading north, take Lanesboro Road and then Railroad Bed East. Follow that dirt road 0.8 miles, bear right onto a narrow dirt track, and park at the gate. Low-clearance cars may prefer to stop at the junction.
vt_marshfield_ledge.approach: From the gate, walk about a mile along the road and take the left fork. Follow the logging road for roughly ten minutes, then turn right onto the climbers trail just before a large boulder and follow it to the base.

va_forest_hill_park.blurb: Forest Hill Park is a city park in Richmond with bouldering gathered in and around Reedy Creek, uphill from the lake. Two main clusters are the Figurehead Wall, at the upstream end, and the Reedy Creek Boulders. It is bouldering only, with a friendly spread of problems from VB up to about V7 and the largest group around V3. The creek corridor makes for a pleasant urban session, and the park is also busy with hikers and mountain bikers, especially on fair weekends. The dirt park trail gets crowded, so weekday mornings are calmer.
va_forest_hill_park.parking_note: Park at the Reedy Creek lot on Riverside Drive, though space is tight on weekends. Another option is to enter from the 41st Street and Stonewall Avenue side near the historic Stone House.

va_eastern_prospectors.blurb: Eastern Prospectors is a sector of the long Prospectors cliffline at Breaks Interstate Park on the Virginia and Kentucky border. The sandstone is hard and compact, often compared to the best Appalachian gorge rock, and the cliff is largely sport climbing with a smaller share of trad. Routes run from the high 5.7s into the 5.12s, with the greatest concentration around 5.10 and 5.11. The terrain mixes slabs, roofs and steeper faces, with the occasional crack. The cliff runs along a hiking trail in a forested setting with long views, so the approach is short.
va_eastern_prospectors.approach: Reach the Prospectors cliffline by trail from either the Tower-Tunnel overlook or the State Line overlook via the Geological Trail; pick the entrance closest to your sector.

wa_world_wall.blurb: World Wall is the high-end sport cliff on the flank of Little Si above North Bend, and one of the top hard sport destinations in Washington. The rock is solid but slick and often steep, so sticky shoes help, and routes run long enough that a 70 meter rope is a good idea. Most climbs fall between 5.11 and 5.13, with a few 5.9 and 5.10 warm-ups and a handful of harder lines. The base is a narrow ledge, so keep dogs and children away from the edge. The wall is shaded by Mount Si early and, in summer, falls into shade around midday, and the overhangs help some lines stay dry in light rain.
wa_world_wall.parking_note: Use the Little Si trailhead lot on Mt Si Road, just past the river bridge, which has vault toilets. It fills early on weekends, and an overflow lot lies to the west.
wa_world_wall.approach: Follow the Little Si Trail about 0.7 miles, until cliffs appear through the trees on your left at the World Wall access trail. This is the part of the hill farthest from the lot.
